skill.displayName: Leaf Curling & Margin Scorch Diagnosis | 植物卷叶/焦边识别（干旱/病害）

llm.summary: The skill is mostly a disclosed cloud plant-diagnosis workflow, but it silently creates or reuses a service identity and stores returned tokens locally, so users should review it before installing.

dimensions.detail: The primary manifest and wrapper script align with plant leaf curling/scorch media analysis and cloud history lookup, but bundled shared code also performs automatic platform login/registration and token handling that goes beyond a narrow image-diagnosis capability.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The manifest discloses automatic cloud queries and internal identity handling, but it instructs the agent not to ask the user for identity details and does not clearly surface that identity fields may be sent to a remote login endpoint during normal use.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No installer, background service, or destructive install behavior was found. A raw private-IP endpoint appears only in a development config while the active config selects production endpoints; the documented module name also appears inconsistent with the packaged script name.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill reads user-provided local media files for upload or submits URLs to a remote service, reads OpenClaw environment identity values, and may read data/smyx-api-key.txt; cloud processing is expected, but the identity-file reuse is sensitive and not clearly user-controlled.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The code creates or reuses a workspace data directory and SQLite database, stores user records plus token/openToken values, and reuses them across runs. No privilege escalation or background persistence was found, but credential-like persistence is material.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable with cloud processing of the provided plant images/videos or URLs, automatic service identity creation/reuse, and local storage of returned service tokens in the workspace data directory. Review the publisher and endpoints, and avoid using sensitive local files as inputs.
llm.findings:
[AST7] expected: The dynamic getattr use is in a local generic DAO helper; it is not shell execution and I did not find a primary workflow path exposing arbitrary filter keys directly to end users, so this is downgraded to an implementation hardening issue.
[LP3] expected: Network access, local file reads, and shell invocation of the packaged Python script are expected for this cloud analysis skill, but permission disclosure is incomplete around identity-file access and token persistence.
[SDI-1] unexpected: The packaged generic smyx_analysis CLI and common helpers are broader than the plant-specific wrapper. The main documented wrapper is plant-specific, so this is not malicious by itself, but it supports the Review verdict for scope overbreadth.
[SDI-4] unexpected: Generic video-analysis wording exists in a bundled helper CLI, while the main manifest and top-level wrapper use plant-diagnosis wording. This is a coherence issue rather than evidence of hidden destructive behavior.
[SDI-2] unexpected: The concern about identity and token handling is supported: the code can read data/smyx-api-key.txt, silently call a remote phoneLogin endpoint with openId/mobile values, and store returned tokens locally.
[SQP-1] expected: Auto-triggering on plant media and history-query phrases is consistent with the manifest, but automatic cloud history lookup without a fresh confirmation is broader than ideal.
[SQP-2] expected: Remote processing of supplied files or URLs is part of the stated workflow, but the artifacts should more plainly disclose file upload, identity transmission, and retention expectations.
[E1] unexpected: External identity transmission is artifact-supported and is the strongest concern; it appears tied to service authentication rather than arbitrary exfiltration, so it does not meet the malicious bar.
[P2] expected: The unicode-control signal resolves to a zero-width joiner in an emoji line, and the operational instructions are visible in SKILL.md; I did not find hidden prompt text.
[YR4] expected: The metadata-poisoning signal appears driven by visible manifest formatting and the same emoji/control-character issue, not by concealed instructions.
[suspicious.install_untrusted_source] unexpected: The raw private-IP endpoint is present in config-dev.yaml, but the active config sets env: prod and uses public lifeemergence.com endpoints, so this is a dormant development artifact rather than active install behavior.
[VirusTotal] expected: VirusTotal telemetry was clean and did not drive the Review verdict.
